newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British Hong Kong legislature boycott in tatters.
newsitem.headline: British Hong Kong legislature boycott in tatters.

text.p: Britain's boycott of a China- appointed legislature in Hong Kong lay in tatters on Wednesday, with even the departing colonial power now contemplating sending an official to the swearing-in ceremony.

The swearing-in of the Provisional Legislature, due to take place within hours of next Monday night's historic handover of Hong Kong to China, will sound the death knell for an elected legislature, formed in elections held in 1995.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will come for the handover ceremony but will stay away from the investiture of the new lawmaking body.
Foreign Office spokesman Bill Dickson indicated in Hong Kong on Wednesday, however, that a British official might go to the ceremony. But he gave no details.
"We're still considering. There's absolutely no prospect of a minister attending, we've made that perfectly clear. But at this stage we're still considering."
Dickson declined to comment on who might represent Britain at the swearing-in. "I don't think I'd like to make any remark about that at this stage," he said.
The outgoing British administration appeared deflated after its biggest ally, the United States, announced overnight that its Hong Kong envoy would attend the gathering.
Britain tried to put on a brave face, shrugging off the U.S. move by noting that at least a U.S. cabinet minister was not partaking in the controversial event.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright reaffirmed in San Francisco she would not go to the investiture but an official said U.S. Consul-General Richard Boucher would be there.
China's decision to replace the Hong Kong legislature with an appointed chamber was "unjustified" and therefore "I will not participate in the swearing-in ceremony", Albright said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Boucher would attend in her stead for reasons of pragmatism.
"(Boucher) has to work, for better or worse, with the new legislature. For practical reasons, he will go."
Asked if London felt let down by Washington's decision, Dickson said: "We don't see it in those terms.
"The Americans will make up their own minds about whether they attend or they're absent.
"I think a ministerial attendance as opposed to an attendance by an official is something quite different."
The president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, Frank Martin, applauded Boucher's attendance.
"It's a step in the right direction and at least symbolically acknowledges the fact that the provisional legislature, whether we agree or disagree, is a fait accompli."

If Britain does attend the swearing-in, it will be the latest in a series of setbacks. On Tuesday, after holding out against Chinese pressure for days, the British caved in and allowed Beijing to send in 500 People's Liberation Army troops three hours before the handover to take up garrison positions.
The European Union envoy in Hong Kong has also predicted European states will boycott the boycott.
But Britain was poised to make a last appeal to Europe to show solidarity against China, the Guardian newspaper in London reported on Wednesday.
Foreign Secretary Cook would make the appeal at a meeting of European Union foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
European diplomats polled by Reuters in Hong Kong said the collapse of the boycott was inevitable.

"It is very difficult to be consistent these days in Hong Kong, either totally moral or totally something else," said one envoy who asked not to be named. "These are strange times in Hong Kong and people are doing what they have to do."
